That bank (book pp.98-111, answers 142-180) sits AFTER all the numbered chapters and is organised by chapter rather than forming part of any chapter's inventory; it is authored into this unit because that is where the question belongs on the paper (founder decision 2026-08-22). SECTION: the heading reads "FUNCTIONS LAQ", so the mark cut is the book's; the seven parts map naturally to seven marks. Printed appearances: TS 17,18,22. Seven parts, and the FIRST decision governs four of them: operations combining f and g are only defined where BOTH are defined, which is the intersection of their domains. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — the bank prints no [N Marks] tags anywhere. The shapes used follow the splits the book DOES print elsewhere: 1+1 for a 2-mark VSAQ (answers 100, 101 on book p.82), 1+1+1+1 or 1+2+1 for a 4-mark SAQ (answers 58, 59 on p.63 and 61 on p.64), and the granular 1x7 for a 7-mark LAQ (answer 32 on p.44). This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Re-cut to the 8-mark Section-C form of the 2026-27 pattern (TGBIE model paper w.e.f. 2026-27): the extra mark goes to Find √f, f² and |f|.

recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — name each move in order.

steps.label: Find the domains
steps.margin_note: Two of the eight marks, and the decision the whole question turns on. f+g exists only where both f and g exist — the intersection {4, 6}, not the union.
steps.memory_tip: f + g exists only where BOTH exist, so the domain is the intersection {4, 6}, never the union.

recall.must_convey: That the domain of a combined function is the INTERSECTION {4, 6}, so only those two preimages are used in parts (i)–(iv).

steps.why: f(5) exists but g(5) does not, so f(5) + g(5) is meaningless. The intersection is not a convention — it is where the sum can actually be computed.
common_mistakes: Using the union and inventing values at 5 and 8.

steps.label: Find f+g, f−g and 2f+4g
steps.margin_note: Two more marks. Evaluate at 4 and 6 only. Watch part (iii): the coefficients multiply the VALUES, so 2f(4) + 4g(4) = 2(5) + 4(−4).
steps.memory_tip: The coefficients multiply the VALUES, not the preimages: 2f(4) + 4g(4) = 2(5) + 4(−4).

steps.why: The preimage never changes — only the value does. 2f means double the OUTPUT at each point, not double the input.
common_mistakes: Subtracting the wrong way round in f−g.

steps.label: Find fg
steps.margin_note: Fifth mark. Multiply the values at each shared preimage.
steps.memory_tip: Multiply the values at each shared preimage — 4 and 6 only.

steps.why: Both products come to −20 by coincidence of the numbers, not by any rule — which is worth checking rather than assuming a slip.
common_mistakes: Using values from the wrong preimages.

steps.label: Find √f, f² and |f|
steps.margin_note: The last three marks. These involve f ALONE, so the domain is f's own {4,5,6} — not the intersection. And √f drops 6, because √(−4) is not a real number.
steps.memory_tip: These use f ALONE, so the domain is f's own {4, 5, 6}. And √f drops 6, since √(−4) is not real.

steps.why: Squaring and taking a modulus work on any real number, but a square root does not work on a negative one. That is why one of the three loses a point and the others do not.
common_mistakes: Using the intersection for these three as well.
